rules.title: Define shared constants when needed
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: A meaningful app-wide value is shared or repeated
rules.rule: Define genuinely shared constants once as static properties on a purpose-named enum when they are needed. Keep Feature-specific values with their owner. Read app identity from bundle metadata when it is authoritative and use localization resources for translatable text. Keep secrets out of app constants.
rules.why: A single definition avoids inconsistent copies while keeping related code easy to find.
rules.verify: Check repeated uses, ownership, bundle metadata, localization and that no secrets are embedded.
rules.example: An AppLinks enum holds the shared company website and support email address.

rules.title: Keep the project structure understandable
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Creating or restructuring a CFA app
rules.rule: Group Views and ViewModels separately from AppModel, Features and their services; retain actual Xcode target membership.
rules.why: Developers can locate capability ownership without following arbitrary layers.
rules.verify: Inspect folders, target membership, resource paths and build configuration.
rules.example: Place NotesEditorView and NotesEditorViewModel together in the View layer, and NotesFeature in the Model layer.

rules.title: Keep business decisions in the Model
rules.section: Maintain an Absolute UI and Model Boundary
rules.applies: Creating or changing UI
rules.rule: Views render and forward intent. A reusable presentation component may receive an action closure that forwards intent to its owning screen and ViewModel. Features own domain decisions and authoritative state.
rules.why: A different device can reuse the same business capability.
rules.verify: Trace reusable component actions to the owning screen and its ViewModel. Verify that the component neither retains a ViewModel nor calls a Feature or service directly. Trace validation, calculations and persistence to their Model owner.
rules.example: A weight screen forwards Save to its ViewModel, which calls the Feature. The Feature validates the value and saves it through its storage service. A reusable RefreshButton can forward the tap through its action closure to the owning screen’s ViewModel.

rules.title: Each screen owns its ViewModel
rules.section: Give Every Unique Screen Its Own ViewModel
rules.applies: Creating or reviewing a SwiftUI screen
rules.rule: A screen owns its dedicated `@State private var viewModel` and constructs it inline by default. A detail screen may initialise its own State-backed ViewModel from selected immutable value data in the View initializer. Do not pass or share ViewModels between Views.
rules.why: Presentation state remains local to the screen.
rules.verify: Inspect screen declarations, navigation destinations, previews and ViewModel construction. Verify that each screen owns its ViewModel and that the stored property is named `viewModel`. Record ownership and naming findings separately.
rules.example: NotesEditorView declares its own private State-backed NotesEditorViewModel.

rules.title: Pass selected values to detail screens
rules.section: Give Every Unique Screen Its Own ViewModel
rules.applies: A destination needs a selected item
rules.rule: A detail View may receive a selected immutable snapshot and use it to construct its own State-backed ViewModel in the View initializer. The snapshot is initial input for that destination identity. Keep selection in presentation and preserve the displayed snapshot and navigation when the source list changes. Use explicit refresh where appropriate. Live updates are a product choice.
rules.why: Each destination can preserve its selection independently.
rules.verify: Open different snapshots in two independently identified destinations. Refresh the source list and verify neither destination silently changes or closes, including when an item is omitted. If the detail offers explicit refresh, verify that it updates only its own display.
rules.example: Next Rocket Launch passes a selected snapshot into its [detail View](https://github.com/3DaysOfSwift/RocketLaunch-iOS-App-Swift-Concurrency/blob/3ecaa30c76428bd8a6f5db8fd5506b6c20b846f7/Swift%20Concurrency%20Project/RocketLaunch/1%20-%20View/Views/Operators/LaunchDetail/LaunchDetailView.swift) and its [ViewModel](https://github.com/3DaysOfSwift/RocketLaunch-iOS-App-Swift-Concurrency/blob/3ecaa30c76428bd8a6f5db8fd5506b6c20b846f7/Swift%20Concurrency%20Project/RocketLaunch/1%20-%20View/Views/Operators/LaunchDetail/LaunchDetailViewModel.swift).

rules.title: Keep view construction and edits local
rules.section: Keep Screen Initializers Clean
rules.applies: Creating screens and editing saved values
rules.rule: Keep blocking I/O, slow work and asynchronous side effects out of View initializers; a detail View may construct its own ViewModel from a selected immutable snapshot. Keep editable text in the screen ViewModel as a separate draft. Submit proposed edits to the responsible Feature. Retain the draft after a failed save and discard it when the user cancels editing.
rules.why: Screen creation remains predictable and cancelled edits do not change authoritative state.
rules.verify: Inspect View initialization for side effects. Fail a save and verify that the editor keeps the draft and the Feature keeps its last confirmed value. Verify that retry publishes the saved replacement only after persistence succeeds. Cancel an unsaved edit and verify it is discarded without a write.
rules.example: An unsaved weight field remains on screen after a failed save and is discarded by Cancel.

rules.title: Define Features by capability
rules.section: Define Features by Business Capability, Not by Screen or Tab
rules.applies: Identifying domain ownership
rules.rule: Features represent business capabilities and own authoritative application state; do not generate a Feature simply for each screen.
rules.why: A Feature can serve multiple screens or targets.
rules.verify: Map actual capabilities and state owners; check that screens consume the Features they need.
rules.example: In the bundled Habit Tracker, HabitsFeature owns saved habits as a capability that multiple screens can use.

rules.title: Compose Features only for real workflows
rules.section: Define Features by Business Capability, Not by Screen or Tab
rules.applies: A business workflow genuinely spans Features
rules.rule: Start with independent Features and inject lower-level services through their initializers. An existing Feature or a distinct coordinating Feature may coordinate other Features when a reusable business responsibility requires it. Keep the dependency direction explicit and acyclic. A screen that only combines existing outputs can do that in its ViewModel.
rules.why: Avoid both feature spaghetti and needless coordinators.
rules.verify: Trace the workflow, verify one owner per state and check dependencies for cycles.
rules.example: A Today capability can coordinate existing Features when its reusable selection decisions belong in the Model. A cohesive CheckoutFeature can own its cart and use a private payment service.

rules.title: Coordinate account changes explicitly
rules.section: Define Features by Business Capability, Not by Screen or Tab
rules.applies: Sign-out, account switching or session expiration affects other Features
rules.rule: UserProfileFeature may call affected Features directly; if sign-out fails before the session ends, retain the session and account data. If authentication reports a partial failure, reconcile the actual session. When a session ends, clear that session’s affected state and report any cleanup failure. After sign-out, a cleanup failure does not restore the ended session. When switching accounts, keep the previous session’s data out of the new session. Check the current account or session generation before publishing an in-flight result, including when the request has been cancelled. Use session identity if a new session for the same account can overlap earlier work. If sign-out promises a fresh-install experience, also clear account-specific memory, caches and locally stored files. Handle unsynchronised work transparently and preserve independent purchases and user-owned documents.
rules.why: A visible direct workflow avoids unnecessary event infrastructure while protecting account data.
rules.verify: Trace sign-out, account switching and external session expiry. Test intact sessions after failed sign-out, cleanup after success, an ended session with failed cleanup, and partial authentication outcomes. Complete an old request after the session changes and verify that it cannot publish, even if cancellation was requested or the same account has signed back in. Check retained data against the product’s sign-out contract.
rules.example: After successful sign-out, UserProfileFeature asks OrdersFeature and FavouritesFeature to clear account data.

rules.title: Compose the application model once per process
rules.section: Use AppModel as the Composition Root and Feature Facade
rules.applies: Composing a CFA app or target
rules.rule: Use one static live() factory to construct production dependencies for AppModel.shared. The explicit initializer assigns supplied concrete Features, sets the launch guard to false, and sets any listener handles to nil. AppModel stores the shared graph, concrete Feature references, one private launch guard, and any private task handles needed for app-wide listeners. The factory injects services into Features without storing the services on AppModel. Keep UI navigation and Feature business rules outside AppModel.
rules.why: The Model has one visible entry point within each process.
rules.verify: Verify that shared is a stored static let using live(). Inspect every other stored property for an allowed role, and check that the explicit initializer supplies its initial value. Confirm that tests supply isolated Features without mutating the production graph.
rules.example: In [NotesReference.swift](../examples/NotesReference.swift), AppModel.live() constructs NotesFeature and its storage dependency for the application graph.

rules.title: Own application-wide listeners at AppModel
rules.section: Use AppModel as the Composition Root and Feature Facade
rules.applies: An event must be observed independent of a screen
rules.rule: When the app needs an event regardless of which screen is visible, AppModel starts its listener once, retains its task handle when asynchronous, and forwards events to the responsible Feature. Define cancellation or replacement when the listener needs it. The Feature interprets events and owns the resulting state. Screen-only observation follows the lifetime of its screen or ViewModel.
rules.why: Lifetime follows the scope that requires the event.
rules.verify: Drive a controlled event source after repeated startup signals. Verify one listener forwards each event to the responsible Feature with no relevant screen mounted. Where cancellation or replacement is supported, verify the old listener stops forwarding and cleanup cannot stop the replacement. Shut down isolated listeners during test cleanup.
rules.example: AppModel owns an app-wide purchase event listener and forwards updates to PurchasesFeature.

rules.title: Share Model code across device targets
rules.section: Use AppModel as the Composition Root and Feature Facade
rules.applies: Adding a widget or another device target
rules.rule: Include shared Model source and only the target’s own Views and ViewModels. Each process has its own AppModel and Features. Adapt composition and platform-specific services without duplicating business rules. An iPhone widget can read an App Group snapshot. With this approach, the iPhone app requests a timeline reload after successfully writing the snapshot. WidgetKit controls when it reloads. A Watch on another device needs a separate snapshot copy through Watch Connectivity or another product-appropriate transfer. The receiving Feature refreshes its own observable state when the change reaches its data source.
rules.why: Capabilities can be reused without assuming shared process memory.
rules.verify: Build each target and check membership and API availability. Verify a successful snapshot write precedes the widget reload request and a failed write issues no request. Test transfer and receiving Feature updates on supported devices separately from builds and controlled tests. Exercise missing, unreadable, delayed or stale data.
rules.example: In the planned Next Rocket Launch showcase, the iPhone writes an App Group snapshot for its widget and then requests a timeline reload. The Watch countdown needs only the next launch, so the phone sends that small snapshot separately through Watch Connectivity. Transfer a larger snapshot file only when the Watch presentation needs it.

rules.title: Preserve deferred destinations
rules.section: Keep Screen Initializers Clean
rules.applies: Handling deep links or notification destinations
rules.rule: For new apps, DeepLinkingFeature records requests to open a URL or notification action, not scheduled or merely delivered notifications. Persist safe pending requests before confirming they are kept. The receiving scene owns navigation, and either scene can open a shared request. Coordinate competing opens and dismissals. Deduplicate repeated callbacks for the same opening event and keep separate events for the same destination distinct. Remove the request after successful navigation or explicit dismissal. Navigation succeeds when the scene opens the destination. Declining, cancelling before navigation or failing to navigate leaves the request pending. The destination loads its own content. If saving the removal fails after navigation, report the failure and retry removal without navigating again. The request may reappear after restart if the removal was never saved. New apps add a separate notification history or global navigation router only when the product requires one. Preserve existing deep-link, notification and history capabilities during migration.
rules.why: The user can keep editing without losing the destination.
rules.verify: Reject invalid destinations before saving. Force an initial save to fail and verify the caller receives the error without an unsaved request appearing in the pending list. Test request reception before restoration completes, preserving both the saved and new requests across restart. Verify refusal, cancellation before and after navigation, competing opens, an open racing dismissal, and dismissal of one request while others remain. Verify that repeated callbacks for the same event do not reopen it and that a distinct event for the same destination remains available. Simulate a failed removal after navigation and verify that retry persists the removal without navigating again. Check that one scene opening a request leaves other scenes’ destinations unchanged.
rules.example: A launch notification remains pending when a user chooses to keep editing; opening its page removes the request.

rules.title: Keep microservices small and well placed
rules.section: Organize Behaviour into Cohesive Features
rules.applies: Choosing or sharing lower-level services
rules.rule: Keep domain-specific services beside their Feature while that location describes their purpose, even when another Feature uses them. Move a broadly applicable service to a shared location when no single Feature naturally owns it. Compose a shared dependency locally in AppModel.live() when common configuration or shared state warrants it, and inject it into its consumers through their initializers. Otherwise use the simplest value or instances that meet the requirements.
rules.why: Organizing code around capability makes it easier to find.
rules.verify: Trace who uses the service and which capability its work belongs to. Check that file placement reflects that responsibility. Verify that a shared instance serves a concrete configuration or state need and reaches its consumers through initializer injection.
rules.example: A launch-specific provider can stay in the schedule folder; a generic network wrapper may move to shared services.

rules.title: Let independent requests progress
rules.section: Organize Behaviour into Cohesive Features
rules.applies: Designing network services
rules.strength: Required unless a documented policy limits concurrency
rules.rule: Keep all URLSession calls in a lower-level NetworkingManager. Feature-specific API adapters validate and decode responses. AppModel may construct the manager in live() for injection without storing it as an AppModel property. Let independent requests progress in parallel unless a documented policy limits them. For new apps, prefer a stateless value type when suitable. An actor may protect shared request state without serializing entire suspended requests.
rules.why: Avoid accidental bottlenecks and data races.
rules.verify: Hold the first response open in a controlled transport and verify that an independent request reaches the transport before the first finishes. Check isolation, request limits and URLSession configuration. Measure suspected bottlenecks before changing the design.
rules.example: Independent launch providers call NetworkingManager for transport and decode their own responses. A provider can start its request while another response is pending.

rules.title: Publish durable edits after saving
rules.section: Keep Persistence Behind Repository Contracts
rules.applies: Saving a user edit or other durable command
rules.rule: Publish confirmed saved state only after required authoritative persistence succeeds. Preserve input on failure. Persist individual record changes by stable identity and reserve whole-dataset replacement for explicit operations with their own integrity rules. For simple preferences, update `UserDefaults` before publishing the value. The setter does not confirm a disk write. Use a storage API that reports the write outcome when the product requires confirmed persistence.
rules.why: The UI must not claim that an unsaved change was saved.
rules.verify: Inject failed and successful writes, then check state and retry behaviour. Reopen storage and verify that overlapping writes to different records preserve both changes.
rules.example: In the bundled Habit Tracker, a failed count save leaves confirmed progress unchanged and TodayViewModel retains the entered value for retry.

rules.title: Use optional snapshots without blocking fresh data
rules.section: Keep Persistence Behind Repository Contracts
rules.applies: Caching replaceable server data
rules.strength: Required when using this cache pattern
rules.rule: Start restoration and refresh independently where both are needed. A missing, incompatible or unreadable cache must not block the download. Publish a current response and complete the refresh for its callers without waiting for the optional cache write. Reject older restores after fresh data arrives, and keep valid in-memory data if refresh fails. Bound cache write retries, preserve an existing good cache on write failure, and prevent older writes from replacing newer snapshots. Claim offline availability only for a saved cache. Use JSON by default when a simple cache is appropriate. Help apply Instant Loading binary snapshots only on request for a stable format with safe decoding. Do not propose binary snapshots during app creation or migration. Durable user edits still require successful persistence before publication as saved.
rules.why: Previously downloaded data can appear quickly without sacrificing fresher server data.
rules.verify: Verify refresh starts with a missing, incompatible or slow cache. Hold the optional cache write pending and verify the response is published and the refresh returns to its callers. Verify that cache write failure leaves fresh results usable, late restoration cannot replace them, and refresh failure retains valid in-memory data. Verify that failed replacements retain the previous cache and delayed writes cannot replace a newer snapshot.
rules.example: In the bundled CFA App template, GitReposFeature publishes a fresh response before its optional cache write completes and rejects an older cache restore.

rules.title: Choose synchronization to match the product
rules.section: Keep Persistence Behind Repository Contracts
rules.applies: An app requires cross-device data or offline edits
rules.rule: Add offline editing or cross-device sync only when the product needs it. For compatible Apple-device data, consider SwiftData with CloudKit or iCloud documents according to the data format. Keep live SwiftData stores out of iCloud Drive. For a custom server, follow its sync contract and use a dedicated sync service when needed. If that workflow supports offline edits, persist the edit and pending-sync metadata together before reporting local success. Report server confirmation separately. Preserve pending changes across failures and restarts, make retries safe against duplication, and define conflict and rejection outcomes with the developer. Apple-managed sync also needs a product decision when multiple devices can edit the same item offline.
rules.why: The simplest storage strategy depends on actual product requirements.
rules.verify: For custom sync, fail the local write and verify that neither local success nor a sendable pending edit is published. After a successful local save, fail sync, restart and retry with the same edit identity to verify one logical server change. When replacing a sync implementation, verify recovery and retry of an edit persisted by the previous version. Exercise conflict and rejection outcomes where applicable. Verify Apple-managed sync, including conflicting offline edits, on supported devices with the required capabilities, account and schema.
rules.example: SwiftData with CloudKit may suit a compatible Apple-device app; a server-backed app follows its server contract.

rules.title: Define task ownership and overlapping-call policy
rules.section: Make Concurrency Behaviour Honest and Visible
rules.applies: Starting asynchronous operations
rules.rule: Define overlap policy at the Feature boundary. By default, equivalent calls share one execution and commands that must each take effect queue in admission order across suspension points, with an outcome for each caller. Decide equivalence from the intended behaviour as well as the inputs. Admit identical inputs separately when each command must take effect. Document the product reason for another policy, such as latest-request-wins. Features own work that must outlive a screen.
rules.why: Task lifetime and repeated actions remain predictable.
rules.verify: Verify equivalent requests share an outcome from one execution. Suspend the first admitted command, then submit further commands, including identical inputs. Verify that each required command executes in admission order, each caller gets its own outcome, and a failure does not strand later commands. Test cancellation, stale results and cleanup.
rules.example: Two equivalent reload callers await the same Feature-owned task. See the bundled Habit Tracker Pro HabitsFeature under 2 - AppModel/Features/Habits.

rules.title: Keep shared refreshes alive across navigation
rules.section: Make Concurrency Behaviour Honest and Visible
rules.applies: A screen leaves during a Feature-owned refresh
rules.rule: By default, the Feature-owned shared refresh continues after a screen leaves, even if that screen was the only caller. Retain successful data and let later equivalent callers join an in-flight request. Awaiting the shared Task handle does not end the wait on caller cancellation. If the screen needs a prompt exit, cancel its wait independently. Use another policy only for a specific product or resource requirement.
rules.why: The user may return and benefit from completed work.
rules.verify: Cancel the only screen waiter and verify the refresh completes and retains its result without a replacement waiter. In a separate case, admit a later equivalent caller while the original refresh is suspended and verify it receives the same outcome without starting another request. Verify that when one of several waiters leaves, the others still receive the result. Where the screen requires prompt cancellation, verify its wait ends while the refresh is still in flight.
rules.example: A schedule refresh continues after the user leaves the screen and its result is available on return.

rules.title: Start the model synchronously
rules.section: Use Application Launch as an Opportunity to Refresh Features
rules.applies: Handling app launch
rules.rule: Call AppModel startup directly and synchronously from the application delegate callback. AppModel signals the relevant Features and starts its app-wide listeners before the callback returns. Features own their asynchronous work, and launch does not wait for disk or network completion. Keep synchronous startup brief and avoid blocking I/O on the main thread.
rules.why: App-wide startup signals are issued before the delegate returns.
rules.verify: Trace the direct call from UIApplicationDelegate through each Feature startup signal and app-wide listener start. Verify repeated callbacks do not repeat startup, and measure first-frame responsiveness separately from network and disk completion. Task creation order alone does not establish I/O start order.
rules.example: The application delegate calls AppModel startup directly; Features start their own asynchronous refreshes.

rules.title: Feature-owned background capabilities
rules.section: Use AppModel as the Composition Root and Feature Facade
rules.applies: Registering iOS background work
rules.rule: Each Feature owns its background capability. During synchronous startup, AppModel can ask the Feature to register its handlers. Register each permitted BGTaskScheduler identifier once before launch finishes and schedule work separately. Route app-level callbacks through AppModel to the responsible Feature and honour expiration, cancellation and system completion. Feature-owned work may outlive a screen. To continue after iOS backgrounds the app, use a supported system mechanism. An ordinary Swift Task grants no background runtime.
rules.why: System lifecycle handling stays separate from feature behaviour.
rules.verify: Verify permitted task identifiers and once-only launch registration. Check that scheduling is separate. Exercise success, failure and expiration individually and verify each completes the system callback exactly once. Verify that expiration cancels owned work. Then deliver expiration while normal completion is pending and verify the race still completes the callback exactly once. Record actual background execution on a supported device separately from controlled tests.
rules.example: AppModel asks a Feature to register an eligible system background handler during launch.

rules.title: Observe authoritative state
rules.section: Use Observation Deliberately
rules.applies: Displaying shared model data
rules.rule: Expose current observable Feature state through a single owner. On supported deployment targets, use `@Observable` for ViewModels and UI-observed Features. Keep Combine where compatibility or publisher composition requires it. Use `@Bindable` only when a control needs a writable binding. A computed ViewModel property can expose Feature state by reading the observable stored value. Use a separate event API where consumers must process every event. Observation alone does not synchronize independent devices or processes.
rules.why: Views can update without creating competing domain state.
rules.verify: Trace the observed property from its Feature owner to the displayed View. When migrating event consumers, verify delivery of repeated values, ordering and cancellation separately from UI state updates.
rules.example: A screen reads its ViewModel's computed property, which reads observable Feature state; the screen updates when that state changes.

rules.title: Check paid capability entry points
rules.section: Preserve One Authoritative Owner for Shared State
rules.applies: A product marks a capability paid
rules.rule: PurchasesFeature owns entitlement state. The screen ViewModel checks current entitlement before presenting or calling the paid capability and otherwise presents the locked or purchase experience. Apply the check at every relevant entry point, including alternative screens and other callers. Keep pricing and entitlement checks out of the capability Feature. Server-protected operations enforce their own authorisation.
rules.why: Pricing changes remain separate from capability behaviour.
rules.verify: Establish which capabilities are paid from product requirements and entitlement policy. Trace every known entry point for paid presentation or execution, and test locked and entitled outcomes on alternate routes as well as the usual screen. Report confirmed unguarded paths with source evidence and their consequence. Mark unresolved paths unverified.
rules.example: An export screen checks PurchasesFeature before presenting or calling the paid export capability.

rules.title: Test architecture at its boundaries
rules.section: Test the Same Boundaries the Architecture Advertises
rules.applies: Implementing or changing CFA behaviour
rules.rule: Give each ViewModel and concrete Feature its own named test file. Test observable behaviour with isolated dependencies and keep AppModel tests separate from the production shared instance. Await Feature commands directly. Verify that equivalent requests share an outcome and separately admitted commands complete in order with individual outcomes. Cover cancellation, stale results and failure recovery where they affect correctness.
rules.why: Tests establish behaviour rather than reproduce implementation details.
rules.verify: Run relevant tests and builds. Use controlled dependencies to verify ordering and outcomes across suspension. Record any checks that could not run.
rules.example: A Feature test injects a failing storage dependency and verifies that the saved value stays unchanged.

rules.title: Preserve product intent
rules.section: Architecture versus product design
rules.applies: Migrating an existing app to CFA and Swift Concurrency
rules.rule: Preserve business outcomes and capabilities while migrating to CFA and Swift Concurrency; fix confirmed in-scope defects and allow necessary minor platform-driven presentation differences without seeking unrelated modernisation.
rules.why: Migration changes how the app works internally without silently removing what users rely on.
rules.verify: Compare the requested journey and business outcomes; test defect fixes and document material platform-driven differences.
rules.example: A migration retains the purchase flow, corrects an in-scope verified defect, and accepts a minor tab bar appearance change required by the platform.

rules.title: Respect project identity
rules.section: Project Identity
rules.applies: Creating or adapting an Xcode project
rules.rule: Follow the project identity rules and user-specified bundle identifier; never change existing identifiers merely to match an example.
rules.why: Identifiers control signing, capabilities and published app continuity.
rules.example: A new target derives its bundle identifier from the product name and requested prefix.
rules.verify: Inspect bundle identifiers across build configurations. For each newly created app target, build for a generic iOS device and verify the built Info.plist contains a resolved bundle identifier, display name, marketing version and build number. Check test target identifiers separately.

rules.title: Maintain template and resource membership
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Editing project layout or templates
rules.rule: Preserve the Xcode template layout contract, resource lookup and target membership.
rules.why: A correct folder tree is not sufficient if Xcode does not compile or bundle the files.
rules.example: A migrated Feature is moved into its proper folder and retained in the intended target.
rules.verify: Inspect the project and build all affected targets.

rules.title: Keep presentation state out of Features
rules.section: Maintain an Absolute UI and Model Boundary
rules.applies: Implementing navigation or display interactions
rules.rule: Keep screen-specific presentation, focus, selection and navigation within the presentation layer.
rules.why: Multiple scenes can present the same model independently.
rules.example: Two launch detail screens retain different selected snapshots.
rules.verify: Review independent windows and navigation while shared data updates.

rules.title: Publish immutable domain snapshots
rules.section: Give Every Unique Screen Its Own ViewModel
rules.applies: Exposing API or persistence data as domain values
rules.rule: Use `let` properties and immutable contents for published snapshot structs. Exclude mutable reference state that could change a snapshot in place. Submit edits through the owning Feature and publish replacement values after authoritative persistence succeeds. For a current server response, publish the new snapshot independently of any optional local cache write.
rules.why: A copy should not diverge by being mutated as though it were authoritative.
rules.example: See the immutable RocketLaunch and nested value types in [Next Rocket Launch](../examples/open-source-apps.md#open-source-ios-apps). The [Notes example](../examples/README.md#notes-reference-feature) shows a confirmed write publishing a new Note.
rules.verify: Check that each stored snapshot property is declared with `let`. Inspect nested values and collection elements for references that can change in place. Trace durable changes through the owning Feature. Verify that a failed write leaves the existing snapshot intact and that a successful write publishes a replacement without changing an earlier snapshot held by a reader.

rules.title: Keep one authoritative Feature owner
rules.section: Preserve One Authoritative Owner for Shared State
rules.applies: Managing shared application state
rules.rule: A single MainActor Feature owns each piece of authoritative shared application state; lower services may own implementation machinery.
rules.why: Callers can identify which component decides the current business state.
rules.example: In the bundled Habit Tracker, HabitsFeature owns saved habits while a repository handles persistence.
rules.verify: Trace reads and writes through all screens and services and check for competing authorities.

rules.title: Avoid an application-wide ViewModel
rules.section: Use AppModel as the Composition Root and Feature Facade
rules.applies: Composing the presentation layer
rules.rule: Keep ViewModels owned by their screens and out of AppModel.
rules.why: AppModel exposes model capabilities without owning UI state.
rules.example: Each screen-level SwiftUI View creates its own ViewModel, which accesses the required concrete Features.
rules.verify: Inspect AppModel properties and the ViewModel ownership tree.

rules.title: Use MainActor for Features
rules.section: Organize Behaviour into Cohesive Features
rules.applies: Defining a CFA Feature
rules.rule: Isolate Feature owners to MainActor; give underlying work an appropriate isolation strategy and avoid expensive blocking work on MainActor.
rules.why: Observable state is coordinated while substantial processing remains responsive.
rules.example: A Feature publishes a decoded schedule returned by a suitably isolated provider.
rules.verify: Inspect isolation annotations and run responsiveness checks where appropriate.

rules.title: Check suspension and stale results
rules.section: Make Concurrency Behaviour Honest and Visible
rules.applies: Updating state across async suspension
rules.rule: Treat await as a possible suspension and check that the operation is still entitled to publish its result.
rules.why: Actor isolation does not make an entire async workflow atomic.
rules.example: In the bundled Habit Tracker Pro starter, PurchasesFeature checks its entitlement revision so an older read cannot overwrite a newer result.
rules.verify: Force out-of-order results and cancellation in controlled tests.

rules.title: Use cancellation to match the work
rules.section: Make Concurrency Behaviour Honest and Visible
rules.applies: Designing task lifetime
rules.rule: Define cancellation at the operation boundary. Cancel superseded presentation work and screen-only work that has no value after departure. Preserve independent shared and durable work according to its ownership policy. Check cancellation before expensive work and again before publishing, and keep obsolete results from overwriting current state.
rules.why: Leaving one screen should not accidentally abandon work needed elsewhere.
rules.example: A superseded search stops while a shared refresh continues.
rules.verify: Cancel a screen waiter while shared work remains active and verify that a later caller can still use the outcome. Complete an obsolete presentation request after its replacement and verify it cannot publish over the current result.

rules.title: Restore safe defaults for obsolete preferences
rules.section: Keep Persistence Behind Repository Contracts
rules.applies: Restoring a non-critical preference
rules.rule: Use a product-defined safe fallback for a missing or obsolete non-critical preference in a recognised format. Preserve the old value where appropriate and replace it only through an intentional migration or a successful user choice. Report unreadable or corrupt durable storage and failed writes as errors.
rules.why: An old theme should not force the user to solve an internal compatibility issue.
rules.example: An unavailable saved colour theme falls back to system appearance.
rules.verify: Test a supported preference, missing and obsolete values, and genuine read and write failures. Verify that fallback preserves the stored value where required.

rules.title: Keep scene navigation independent
rules.section: Keep Screen Initializers Clean
rules.applies: Opening a link or notification in a multi-window app
rules.rule: Route each destination through a scene-appropriate handler without putting scene navigation state inside DeepLinkingFeature.
rules.why: A link should not unexpectedly redirect another window.
rules.example: A Settings screen asks the Feature to open its pending item in the receiving scene.
rules.verify: Verify that either scene can open a pending request and that simultaneous attempts navigate only once. A successful open removes the shared item while preserving the other scene’s navigation. Declined navigation or an unavailable scene leaves the request pending.

rules.title: Keep unsaved field edits in the ViewModel
rules.section: Preserve One Authoritative Owner for Shared State
rules.applies: Editing unsaved field values on a screen
rules.rule: Keep the unsaved field value in the screen ViewModel until a save succeeds or the user cancels; retain it after a failed save. Persisted values remain Feature-owned.
rules.why: An abandoned edit does not become shared application state.
rules.example: A weight editor keeps the entered number after a failed save.
rules.verify: Exercise save, failure, retry and Cancel without mutating the Feature early.

rules.title: Inject volatile dependencies
rules.section: Keep Time and Other Volatile Dependencies Injectable
rules.applies: Business decisions depend on time or another changing external value
rules.rule: Supply volatile dependencies in a controllable form rather than hiding them in business decisions.
rules.why: Time-dependent behaviour can be reproduced in tests.
rules.example: A countdown decision uses an injected clock.
rules.verify: Test boundary dates and time zones using controlled inputs.

rules.title: Use readable Feature commands
rules.section: Organize Behaviour into Cohesive Features
rules.applies: Designing a Feature API
rules.rule: Expose domain-oriented operations and values instead of deep storage graphs or generic mechanics.
rules.why: Callers can understand what a capability does from its API.
rules.example: A weight Feature exposes a named operation to save an entry.
rules.verify: Read call sites and check they do not manipulate repositories or nested implementation state.

rules.title: Prefer straightforward change
rules.section: Prefer Readable Domain Language over Architectural Ceremony
rules.applies: Implementing or migrating code
rules.rule: Choose the simplest structure that preserves necessary behaviour, ownership and safety.
rules.why: Fewer unnecessary layers improve comprehension and maintenance.
rules.example: A sign-out workflow uses direct Feature calls instead of a new event bus.
rules.verify: Trace the whole workflow and remove scaffolding with no demonstrated purpose.

rules.title: Handle failures honestly
rules.section: Keep Persistence Behind Repository Contracts
rules.applies: Storage, network or business work fails
rules.rule: Report the outcome of the work the user requested. If a durable save fails, retain the draft and previously confirmed state and expose a recoverable error. If an optional cache write fails after a successful download, keep the fresh data visible and avoid claiming offline availability.
rules.why: The user needs to know whether an operation succeeded.
rules.example: An unsuccessful durable save leaves the editor available for retry.
rules.verify: Inject failures and verify displayed outcomes and state.

rules.title: Keep the dependency flow explicit
rules.section: Layered Architecture
rules.applies: Designing or reviewing application structure
rules.rule: Keep the relationship View → ViewModel → Feature → Microservices; AppModel composes and exposes Features.
rules.why: Dependencies follow clear ownership instead of scattered business decisions.
rules.example: A screen ViewModel asks a schedule Feature, which calls a networking microservice.
rules.verify: Trace a user operation through each layer and inspect reverse dependencies.

rules.title: Coordinate without unnecessary layers
rules.section: Coordinated Application Flow
rules.applies: Implementing a feature workflow
rules.rule: Keep the cooperating parts connected by clear responsibilities and avoid bypassing the Feature that owns a business action.
rules.why: The execution path remains understandable and testable.
rules.example: A refresh reaches the schedule Feature before its provider.
rules.verify: Trace the entry point, owners, state changes and dependencies.

rules.title: Separate domain and display decisions
rules.section: Separate Domain Decisions from Display Decisions
rules.applies: Formatting or presenting Feature results
rules.rule: Features decide domain meaning; ViewModels translate results for display and Views render them.
rules.why: Business decisions stay reusable across devices.
rules.example: A Feature determines a domain result and the ViewModel prepares its display label.
rules.verify: Inspect calculations and business classification for leaks into Views and ViewModels.

rules.title: Apply CFA governing principles
rules.section: Governing Principles
rules.applies: Building or reviewing a CFA app
rules.rule: Use the governing ownership, Swift Concurrency and readability principles together rather than applying one in isolation.
rules.why: Individual conventions are meaningful only as a coherent architecture.
rules.example: A shared Feature owns state and exposes operations to multiple dedicated ViewModels.
rules.verify: Review Feature boundaries, isolation and the full source principles.

rules.title: Avoid complexity without product value
rules.section: Maintenance over Complexity
rules.applies: Adding an abstraction or migration layer
rules.rule: Keep structures simple enough to understand while preserving real behaviour and safety.
rules.why: Unnecessary layers obscure the system and increase maintenance cost.
rules.example: A small sign-out workflow makes explicit Feature calls instead of adding an event bus.
rules.verify: Identify each layer’s concrete responsibility and remove unjustified duplication.

rules.title: Apply the full conformance checklist
rules.section: Review Checklist
rules.applies: Auditing a CFA implementation
rules.rule: Review the complete checklist against the actual app and report findings with evidence.
rules.why: A single passing rule cannot establish whole-app conformance.
rules.example: An audit checks ViewModel ownership, Feature state and task lifetimes.
rules.verify: Trace each applicable checklist item and distinguish unverified behaviour from passes.

rules.title: Avoid prohibited CFA patterns
rules.section: Prohibited Patterns
rules.applies: Implementing or auditing CFA code
rules.rule: Check the full prohibited-pattern list and its applicable context.
rules.why: Known architecture violations should not survive as isolated exceptions.
rules.example: A View does not receive another screen’s ViewModel.
rules.verify: Search source and target membership, then verify actual usage and tests.

rules.title: Create focused test targets
rules.section: Project Identity
rules.applies: Creating an Xcode project
rules.rule: Create a unit-test target; add a UI-test target only for a specifically requested UI automation scenario.
rules.why: Empty test targets add noise without evidence.
rules.example: A new project has Feature and ViewModel unit tests.
rules.verify: Inspect targets and run the relevant unit tests.

rules.title: Keep the template layout and assets correct
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Creating or editing the CFA Xcode template
rules.rule: Keep App.swift, the root asset catalog and app resources in their prescribed locations and maintain Xcode navigator references.
rules.why: A template must produce a usable project with the expected structure.
rules.example: A StoreKit configuration stays in App Resources and remains linked from its scheme.
rules.verify: Run the template structure verifier and inspect a generated project.

rules.title: Do not create dumping-ground folders
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Organising files
rules.rule: Use folder names that describe the responsibility of their contents rather than vague catch-all folders.
rules.why: Related implementation remains easy to locate.
rules.example: A networking helper lives with the networking capability rather than a generic Helpers folder.
rules.verify: Inspect folder names and the actual responsibilities of their contents.

rules.title: Apply optional visual defaults only in scope
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Shaping a new app or changing an existing product
rules.rule: Use new-product visual defaults when applicable and preserve existing approved designs during maintenance.
rules.why: An architecture task should not silently redesign an existing product.
rules.example: Do not add a CFA Settings footer to an established app unless the request or workflow calls for it.
rules.verify: Compare UI changes with user instructions and the product design authority.

rules.title: Validate device orientation configuration
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Creating an iOS app or preparing its archive
rules.rule: Declare supported orientations in each configuration and inspect the built or archived Info.plist; honour explicit product choices.
rules.why: A simulator build alone does not prove archive configuration or layout compatibility.
rules.example: A universal app declares appropriate iPhone and iPad orientations.
rules.verify: Build Release for a generic iOS device and inspect the built orientation arrays. When preparing an archive, inspect its app plist too. Exercise supported rotation and iPad resizing before claiming UI compatibility.

rules.title: Organise extensions and domain types by purpose
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Adding Swift extensions or domain values
rules.rule: Follow the specification’s placement rules for extensions and keep domain types with their semantic owner.
rules.why: Related types remain understandable independently of storage representation.
rules.example: A launch snapshot belongs with the launch capability rather than being defined by its database schema.
rules.verify: Review extension and type ownership against the full source section.

rules.title: Keep SwiftUI construction fast
rules.section: Give Every Unique Screen Its Own ViewModel
rules.applies: Constructing a SwiftUI View or ViewModel
rules.rule: Avoid blocking I/O, slow work and asynchronous side effects in initializers and body construction.
rules.why: SwiftUI may construct Views repeatedly and must remain responsive.
rules.example: A ViewModel is initialized cheaply and asks its Feature to start work through a named method.
rules.verify: Inspect initializers and measure slow paths where needed.

rules.title: Retain ViewModel-owned unstructured tasks
rules.section: Make Concurrency Behaviour Honest and Visible
rules.applies: A ViewModel creates an unstructured Task
rules.rule: Retain a named handle for each independently managed unstructured operation the ViewModel creates. Reuse the active handle for equivalent actions when one execution satisfies each caller. Commands that must each take effect keep their own outcomes. Clear the handle after publishing the outcome on success, failure or cancellation. Framework-owned lifecycle tasks and structured children keep their existing owners.
rules.why: Task ownership and shared completion stay visible.
rules.example: Repeated refresh taps return the same active ViewModel task handle. An async caller awaits its value when it needs completion. The Feature still coordinates equivalent requests from other screens.
rules.verify: Verify equivalent callers share one execution and observe its completion. Test cleanup after success, failure and cancellation, including that an obsolete task cannot clear a replacement handle.

rules.title: Never gate UI on database availability
rules.section: Use Application Launch as an Opportunity to Refresh Features
rules.applies: Launching when persistence is slow or unavailable
rules.rule: Install stable root navigation independently of store availability. Initializers and AppModel.live() assemble dependencies. The storage owner opens the store lazily on a Feature request and prepares the configured parent directory before opening a file-backed store. The affected screen presents directory or opening errors and retries the same domain request through its ViewModel and Feature. Retry can attempt an open that never succeeded. Reuse a successfully opened store when a fetch fails. Preserve the configured location and existing data. An unsuccessful initial fetch must surface a failure, while a failed refresh preserves previously loaded data.
rules.why: Users can access unaffected capabilities and see honest loading or failure states.
rules.example: The root screen appears while a Feature restores local data.
rules.verify: Hold store opening pending, then fail it. Verify the root stays visible, an unaffected destination remains accessible, and the affected screen explains the failure and can retry successfully without replacing the root or losing saved data. In a separate case, fail a fetch after opening and verify retry reuses the working store and preserves any prior results. Verify actual store opening and UI behaviour separately from controlled tests.

rules.title: Keep the SwiftUI App entry point structural
rules.section: Use Application Launch as an Opportunity to Refresh Features
rules.applies: Implementing the SwiftUI App entry point
rules.rule: Keep the App structure focused on scene composition and use the application lifecycle for the synchronous AppModel launch signal.
rules.why: Startup ownership remains independent of any one View.
rules.example: The app delegate invokes AppModel directly before returning from launch.
rules.verify: Inspect App.body, root navigation and the delegate. Verify a stable root per scene, no storage-dependent root branches, and a direct synchronous launch signal from the delegate. Screen lifecycle tasks may start their own work, while shared startup belongs to AppModel.
